note:
v1, CARRYING CAPACITY: the sixth song, a skeleton (the whole shape, played bare). You said "make it unique"; this is what I took that to mean, and it is yours to overrule.
THE IDEA: I did not write a riff. The song has one rule and one dial. The rule is the oldest model of a population (next year's number is this year's, times how fast it breeds, times the room left). It is worked out once every half bar, and the number it gives IS that half bar: how many of its six places the band strikes, where the accent falls, how high the accent is. The form is only the dial being turned up and brought back down:
- 0:00 it grows from nothing to a plain shuffle, and stays there: the same half bar every time (0:14);
- 0:28 it splits: two half bars that take turns; 0:42 four; 0:56 eight (the riff doubles its own length);
- 1:10 it stops repeating altogether, and is still plainly the same riff;
- 1:27 it LOCKS, by itself, on a cycle five half bars long; 1:58 on three; 2:14 on six. Nobody chose five or three: they are in the rule. Against a bar of two they are this record's odd meters, found and not written;
- 2:24 the dial is at the top: it screams, then there is nothing at all for a bar or more (after its highest number the rule always gives its lowest), and a long low boom falls through the hole; then it climbs back;
- 2:52 the dial comes down through four, two, one, and at 3:13 the song dies out on three single notes.
HOW IT IS UNLIKE THE OTHER FIVE: it is in triplets (the others are in straight sixteenths) and faster (138; they are 100 to 126); on E (they sit on F and C); its drums are a DRUM MACHINE, new on this record; and the tune on top is not written in the song at all. That track holds only the rule, and the engine works the notes out itself (a feature no song here had used); I checked its 171 notes against mine and none differ.

WHAT I MEASURED (I cannot listen): compscore 72.30 / 82.65 (seeds 0 and 11). 3:23 long. Against the eleven records the balance is within about 2 dB in every band but the lowest, in the four stretches I read.
WHAT IS BARE OR WRONG, and I know it:
- From 0:41 to 2:24 the band is at one level (within 0.6 dB). The riff changes under it and the arrangement does not yet: that is the next rounds' work.
- Nothing comes back but the short run down at the end, and the scorer marks that hard (its lowest term). It may have a point: whether the song wants a real return is open.
- The two seeds score ten points apart: the scorer cannot find this song's sections reliably yet.
- The guitars and the bass are Running Total's. This song has no sound of its own yet but the machine and the chip lead.
- The drum machine has been levelled in the mix three times and never tuned by ear: it has no room and no body like the kit's.
WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether a drum machine and a shuffle belong on this record, and whether you can hear the riff split without being told.
ONE CARD, because it decides the song: the drum machine (ten seconds of it).
NOT HEARD BY ANYONE.

v2, WHAT A BAND CAN DO ONCE THE RIFF REPEATS (section round, as drawn: 1:51-2:19, where the rule locks on three half bars; the map called it static).
While the rule never repeats, nobody can arrange it: every half bar is news, so the whole band plays it together. Where it locks, the same three half bars come round again and again, and a band that has heard a riff twice starts to arrange it. v1 played the window exactly like the stretches round it. Now it is told a layer at a time:
- 1:58 the dial moves, and for three half bars the rule is still finding the cycle. The snare keeps the back beat it had. At 2:01, on the cycle's first scream, a cymbal marks it and the snare drops to half time: the groove changes when the rule locks, not when I turn the dial.
- 2:04, second time round: the cycle has a hole in it (one low note, then most of a half bar of nothing). A second chip answers there with the cycle's own three notes played as one quick triplet, the cycle inside itself; its last note is the note the band plays next.
- 2:06, third time round: the second pair of guitars takes the scream a third higher, so the scream is a four-note chord.
- Both carry on through the six (2:14) to the top of the dial (2:24).

(2) The answering chip's last note is the ACCENT of the half bar that follows (two octaves up), not the band's very next note, which is a muted low E. The rest stands.

v3, THE BAND TELLS YOU WHERE THE RULE IS (whole-song round, as drawn).
Through v2 the riff changed under a band that did not: from 0:41 to 2:24 the song sat within 0.6 dB, four guitars and the same hat whether the rule was repeating or running wild. And the run down at the end moved the dial every four bars, before the rule had settled: the stretch I called "four" never once played its four half bars through. Three changes, one idea:
1. THE WALL AND THE OPEN HAT ARE FOR NEWS. Where the rule repeats, the band is two guitars and a closed hat: a riff you know, played tight. Where it does not repeat, the second pair of guitars comes in and the hat opens on every beat. So the song now steps where the rule changes state: up at 1:10 (it stops repeating), down at 1:27 (it locks on five: the leanest thing in the middle of the song), up at 1:44, down at 2:01 (it locks on three) and built back a layer at a time, as in v2, except that the second pair of guitars now ARRIVES with the harmony the third time round (2:06).
2. THE TOP: at the top of the dial (2:24) every scream has the cymbal on it, ringing into the hole that follows.
3. THE DIAL COMES DOWN SLOWLY ENOUGH TO HEAR (2:52). Four: six seconds of the rule finding it, then the two-bar riff twice. Two (3:06). Then one (3:16): the shuffle of 0:14 comes home for six bars, its accent still rocking between two places as the rule settles, and at 3:27 the song dies out as before. The song is 3:37 (it was 3:23).

- The steps, in the finished file: +0.9 dB at 1:10, -0.8 at 1:27, +1.3 at 1:44, -1.1 over the lock at 2:01, +1.0 at 2:06. Before, all of that was within 0.6 dB.

- Against the eleven records the open hat first read 3 dB too bright in the stretches it fills; I took it down 3 dB and it reads about 1.5 over.
WORSE OR NOT ACHIEVED, and I know it:
- THE TOP IS NOT LOUDER than the other two stretches that do not repeat (where it sounds, it reads 0.1 dB over them). It is marked by the cymbals and the holes, not by size.
- The first minute is now two guitars from 0:14 to 1:10. The riff doubling its length at 0:42 and 0:56 is the only event there; the second pair used to come in at 0:42. If the first minute sags, that is the cost of saving the wall for 1:10.
- At home (3:16) the shuffle's accent alternates between two places and does not sit still as it did at 0:14: the rule is still settling when the song ends.

note:
v4, THE WAY UP HAS EVENTS, AND THE TOP IS THE SUM (a whole-song round on Carrying Capacity. The draw gave Running Total, a section round: the same window I passed on at 12:21, and I still have nothing for it I would defend unheard; this song had two costs I named an hour ago, so I took it instead).
The costs of v3 were: the first minute on two guitars with nothing happening at 0:42 and 0:56 but the riff doubling its length; and a top (2:24) at which the band dropped what it had just learned. Three small things:
1. THE HAT COUNTS FINER AS THE RIFF GETS LONGER. While the riff is one or two half bars long the machine's hat is on the beat. When it becomes four half bars (0:42) the hat plays the shuffle's four places; when it becomes eight (0:56) it runs, all six. At 1:10 it opens, on the beat, with the wall.
2. EIGHT IS A RIFF SAID TWICE, and a band arranges a repeat: the second time (1:03) the tune has a second voice a third above it. Like the tune, it is not written: the engine works it out from the rule.
3. THE TOP KEEPS WHAT THE SONG HAS LEARNED: the screams stay four-note chords, as they became at 2:06; and where the three's shape turns up again inside the chaos (a scream, then one low note: it does, twice, at 2:31 and 2:39) the chip answers as it did in the window.

- These are small changes by measurement, and I say so: the loudness of every stretch is as it was (within 0.1 dB). The hat sits 14 dB under the band; its finer count is the smallest of the three.
- The second voice reads 3.7 dB under the tune. First level, not re-tried.
- The top end against the records moved from 0.9 to 1.5 dB over where the hat plays four, and 1.8 where it runs.
STILL TRUE: the top is no louder than the other stretches that do not repeat. And the first minute is still two guitars; if it sagged before, a hat and eight bars of a second voice may not be enough to hold it.
WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether a running hat reads as the machine winding up, or as busy.
